concepts.label: Science as Exploration
concepts.cardText: In the middle stage science invited you to be curious, observe the world closely and ask questions. At the secondary stage the journey continues with an emphasis on deep exploration. Science is not only about what we know, but also about how we know it: how observations lead to measurements, how patterns are expressed using symbols and equations, how models are built to represent complex systems, and how ideas are tested, often revised, and sometimes even discarded. The page numbers are framed by a magnifying glass, which symbolises careful observation, and a compass, which reminds us that exploration needs direction: choosing appropriate models, asking the right questions and knowing the limits of where ideas apply. Exploration in science is not wandering aimlessly but trying to make sense of the world with care and purpose.

concepts.label: Models in Science
concepts.cardText: The natural world is complex and studying it in full detail is often impossible, so science uses models: simplified ways of looking at real systems that focus only on what is most important for a given question. In physics a moving car may be represented as a single point, in chemistry atoms and molecules are drawn as spheres and bonds, in biology cells are shown as diagrams highlighting key parts, and in earth science the Earth may be treated as a smooth sphere layered into distinct regions. Building models involves making assumptions and deliberately ignoring certain details; for example air resistance may be neglected to understand the basic effect of gravity, and when studying how the heart pumps blood many individual cells are ignored. These choices are not mistakes; they are done on purpose to keep things simple enough while still allowing us to find answers.

concepts.label: Example: Modelling a Cricket Shot
concepts.cardText: To model a cricket ball hit for a six, ask whether the ball will cross the boundary without hitting the ground first. For this, the brand of the bat, the colour of the ball and the amount of grass on the field make no difference, but the mass of the ball and the speed and direction in which it has been hit are very important. Air resistance, the spin of the ball and the stitching of the seam have smaller effects that can be ignored in a simple model. As we build more complex models we add extra details for greater accuracy.

concepts.label: Simplifying the Stars: Meghnad Saha
concepts.cardText: Science often begins by ignoring details. When the physicist Meghnad Saha studied the light from stars, he did not try to model every atom, every reaction or every movement inside a star. Instead he treated the matter in the star as a hot gas, ignored many complex processes, and focused only on temperature, pressure and how atoms formed ions. This simplification allowed him to explain how the colour of stars is deeply connected to their temperature.

concepts.label: Precise Language, Symbols and Units
concepts.cardText: Science uses language in a very careful and precise way. Many everyday words, such as force, work, cell or reaction, have specific meanings in science, and these meanings are specific because scientific ideas must be communicated clearly and unambiguously. To allow scientists across the world to describe observations, compare results and build ideas together, science uses a shared language of specific terms, symbols and units. Quantities such as mass, velocity, force and electric current are represented by symbols like m, v, F and I, each associated with a defined unit.

concepts.label: Mathematics in Science
concepts.cardText: Science often turns to mathematics to allow relationships between quantities to be expressed clearly and tested carefully. Mathematics in science is not meant to be a hurdle; it is a language that helps us think more clearly about the world. An equation is not just a calculation tool, it is a compact statement about how certain things are related. Describing motion using distance, time and velocity lets us answer where an object will be at a later moment, and mathematical expressions describe rates of chemical reactions, patterns of population growth or changes in energy. Learning to use mathematics in science does not mean memorising equations; it means understanding the situation first, identifying relevant quantities and then using mathematical relationships to reason carefully, so mathematics becomes a powerful language for thinking, not just for finding numerical answers.

concepts.label: Standard Units: Why Is a Kilogram Used Everywhere?
concepts.cardText: A kilogram should mean the same amount everywhere when we buy rice or vegetables, and measurements are based on agreed international standards, not local objects or opinions. Standard units allow scientific results to be compared and ensure fairness in daily life and trade. In a well-known incident a passenger aircraft ran out of fuel mid-flight because of a mix-up in units: the ground crew used the density of fuel in pounds per litre rather than kilograms per litre, leaving the aircraft about 15,000 litres short, and it had to glide to an emergency landing. Using standard (SI) units everywhere avoids conversions and errors. Scientific symbols often come from history and international agreement; the speed of light is denoted c from the Latin word celeritas, meaning speed.

concepts.label: Laws, Theories and Principles
concepts.cardText: As observations are repeated, measurements refined and ideas tested through experiments, we can organise our understanding of the world in a systematic way. A law usually describes a regular pattern observed in nature, often expressed in words or mathematical relationships; for example Newton's laws of motion explain the jerk felt when a bus stops suddenly. A theory goes a step further and provides an explanation of why those patterns occur, usually based on evidence gathered over time; for example the atomic theory explains how molecules are formed. Principles are broad ideas that help us make sense of a given situation; for example the principle of conservation of energy applies when climbing up the stairs. In science a theory does not mean a guess or an untested idea; it is an explanation based on careful testing and critical examination, always open to improvement and often changing as new evidence becomes available, which is a key feature that makes science reliable.

concepts.label: Prediction in Science
concepts.cardText: One of the most remarkable strengths of science is its ability to make predictions. When laws, theories and models are well established, they allow us to anticipate what will happen under new or different conditions, before we can perform an experiment and in many cases even if we cannot. Using ideas about motion we can predict how far a kicked football will travel; using chemical reactions we can estimate how much carbon dioxide will be produced; using biological principles we can predict how breathing changes while running. These predictions are not guesses; they are reasoned expectations based on evidence and careful thinking. When predictions match observations, confidence in the underlying science grows, and even more important, when they do not, scientists re-examine their assumptions, models or measurements. In this way prediction is a powerful tool that drives further exploration and deeper understanding.

concepts.label: Checking Predictions Scientifically
concepts.cardText: Varsha told Meghna that it will rain this afternoon because the clouds look dark. To make the prediction scientifically testable, Meghna should ask for measurable evidence and past patterns, not simple yes/no questions. She could ask what the condition of the sky was when it rained last time, what the humidity is today and whether it was above 80 per cent the last time it rained, what the wind speed and direction are, and whether the temperature is dropping as it did before the recent rains. These questions ask about measurable data and past patterns, which go beyond the mere observation that the clouds look dark. Weather forecasts sometimes go wrong because weather depends on many changing factors such as temperature, pressure, humidity and wind, and very tiny differences in conditions can grow over time and lead to something completely different, so forecasts are usually reliable for a few hours or days but less certain further ahead.

concepts.label: Limits of Theories and Evidence-Based Thinking
concepts.cardText: Even the most successful scientific theories have limits and may fail when new conditions are explored or when measurements become more precise. Such failures are not a weakness of science; in fact, they are its greatest strength. When predictions do not match observations, scientists do not reject ideas based on opinion or belief, but only on evidence. No scientific theory is ever final and none is beyond question; this openness to being corrected by nature itself is what has allowed science to help us understand the world. The same habit helps us check viral claims on social media, such as that food becomes harmful during an eclipse: an eclipse is just a play of shadows, and asking simple scientific questions about what physical change occurs, whether temperature changes significantly or food goes bad in a shadow, shows that no physical, chemical or biological mechanism supports such a claim.

concepts.label: Estimation and Approximate Reasoning
concepts.cardText: A helpful strategy is to first understand the situation being studied, then identify the quantities that matter, and finally make a rough estimate to check whether an answer makes sense. Exact values are not always necessary, especially in the early stages of reasoning; an approximate estimate is often enough to tell whether a result is reasonable or impossible. Estimating helps build intuition, detect errors and develop confidence, and science values careful reasoning perhaps much more than accurate calculations. For example, in estimating how much rice would feed a family of four for a month, the aim is not an exact number but to check that the answer makes sense, since 100 g for a month is clearly too little while a few tonnes is far too much. To estimate the air breathed in a day, take about 12-15 breaths a minute over 1440 minutes, roughly 20 thousand breaths, and about 0.5 litre per breath (it takes 4-5 breaths to fill a 2-litre balloon), giving about 10,000 litres a day.

concepts.label: Branches of Science and Connections Across Disciplines
concepts.cardText: After Grade 10, if you study science, it will be divided into branches like physics, chemistry, biology and earth science, and even in Grades 9 and 10 the chapters focus on some of these areas. But the natural world does not have such boundaries; these divisions are made by us only to help organise knowledge, and they are not independent of each other. Most real-world problems, such as understanding climate change, developing medicines or designing sustainable technologies, require ideas from several disciplines together, and science also connects naturally with mathematics, technology, arts and social sciences. To make sense of the world fully we need to connect multiple ways of knowing and expressing ideas, each enriching the other. For example, understanding how a mask works needs physics (particle motion and electrostatic attraction), chemistry (properties of polymer fibres), biology (size and behaviour of viruses) and mathematics (modelling airflow and filtration efficiency).

concepts.label: Science as a Human Activity
concepts.cardText: Science is not just a collection of facts, equations or experiments. It is a human activity shaped by curiosity, creativity, collaboration and careful questioning. It grows as people ask questions, test ideas, share results and learn from mistakes, and develops over time through the work of many individuals across different cultures and generations. Even if you do not study science beyond Grade 10, scientific thinking will be very important in whatever you do: it helps you understand the technology around you, evaluate information critically and make sense of the world. Science invites you not only to learn about the world but to learn how we are trying to understand it.
